passages.t: ‘Deep sorrow’: Paul's grief for his own people
passages.happening:
Romans 8 ended with a shout of confidence: nothing can separate God's people from his love. Now the tone drops. Paul begins chapters 9 to 11 with an oath and with tears.

“I speak the truth in Christ; I am not lying, as confirmed by my conscience in the Holy Spirit” (verse 1). “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (verse 2). Why? Most of his own people, the Jews, have not believed that Jesus is the Messiah, the King God promised.

Then Paul says something startling. “For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood” (verse 3).

He lists what belongs to Israel. “Theirs is the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants; theirs the giving of the law, the temple worship, and the promises” (verse 4). Theirs are the patriarchs, the fathers of the nation, and from them comes Christ himself, as far as his human descent goes (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The house churches in Rome had both Jewish and Gentile members. Gentiles are people who are not Jewish. Some Gentile believers may have begun to think that God had finished with Israel. Paul does not start by arguing. He starts by grieving.

Notice what he does not say. He does not say ‘they’ with a curl of the lip. He says ‘my brothers, my own flesh and blood’. He is a Jew speaking about his own family. Everything that follows in these three chapters is spoken in that voice.

The list in verses 4 and 5 is a list of treasures, and every item is still in the present tense: ‘theirs is’. ‘Adoption as sons’: God called Israel his firstborn son. ‘The divine glory’: God's presence that filled the tabernacle and the temple. ‘The covenants’: God's binding promises to Abraham, to Israel at Sinai, and to David. ‘The giving of the law’: the teaching God gave through Moses. ‘The temple worship’: the sacrifices and prayers in Jerusalem. ‘The promises’: all God had pledged to do.

The patriarchs are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The last gift is the greatest. The Messiah himself is a Jew. A Gentile believer in Rome could not look down on Israel without looking down on the family of Jesus.
passages.ot:
Paul's wish to be cursed for his people has one clear model in the Old Testament. After Israel worshipped the golden calf, Moses prayed for them, “Yet now, if You would only forgive their sin” (Exodus 32:32), and then, if not, “please blot me out of the book that You have written” (Exodus 32:32). Moses was willing to lose his own place to save his people. Paul stands where Moses stood.

The first gift, being God's son, comes from the exodus. God told Moses to say to Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). Paul used the same word, adoption, for every believer in Romans 8:15. He does not take it away from Israel to give it to the church. Both stand in this letter side by side.
passages.hard:
Two hard things sit in these verses.

The first is Paul's wish. Could anyone really choose to be cut off from Christ? Paul knows he cannot be, for he has just said nothing can separate believers from God's love (8:38-39). ‘I could wish’ is the language of a wish that cannot be granted. It shows how much he loves his people. That love is the key to reading the hard argument that follows.

The second is the end of verse 5. The Berean Standard Bible reads, “Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise” (verse 5). Its footnote offers another way to put the last words of praise. The oldest Greek copies have almost no punctuation, so the question is where to put a comma or a full stop. With a comma, the words describe Christ: he is God over all. That is how most modern translations, and most early Christian writers, read it. With a full stop after ‘Christ’, the words become a separate blessing of God the Father, as some translations print it. Readers who take the first view note that Paul's blessings usually attach to someone just named, as in Romans 1:25. Readers who take the second note that Paul rarely calls Christ ‘God’ in so many words. The church's belief that Christ is God does not hang on this one verse (see John 1:1 and 20:28).
passages.asks: Paul's hardest argument begins with tears, not a lecture. Think of a question about God that you argue over with others. Ask whether you could hold it as Paul held this one: with love for the people you disagree with, and grief more than scorn.

passages.t: ‘God's word has not failed’: Isaac, Jacob and Esau
passages.happening:
Paul now states his claim. “It is not as though God’s word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel” (verse 6).

Being Abraham's descendant has never been the whole story, Paul says. Abraham had more than one son, but God said, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (verse 7). So it is “the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring” (verse 8). The promise was, “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son” (verse 9).

Then Paul goes a step further. Rebecca's twins had the same father and the same mother. Yet before they were born or had done anything good or bad, God's plan of election stood, “not by works but by Him who calls” (verse 12). She was told, “The older will serve the younger” (verse 12). And Scripture says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘Election’ means God's choosing. Paul's point in these verses is about who God's people have always been. From the very start, God worked through a line of promise, not simply through everyone born into the family.

A Jewish hearer knew the stories well. Abraham's first son was Ishmael, born to Hagar. But the promise ran through Isaac, Sarah's son, born when it seemed impossible. Isaac's wife Rebecca bore twins, Esau and Jacob. In that world the older son normally received the larger share and the leading place. God reversed the order: the younger would lead.

So when Paul says ‘not all who are descended from Israel are Israel’, he is not saying Israel has been cancelled. He is saying something Israel's own Scriptures had shown many times: God's promise moves by his calling and mercy. Within Israel there has always been a faithful core who trusted the promise.

‘Not by works’ in verse 12 means not by anything the twins had done. God's choosing came first. That is the thread Paul will follow: mercy is never earned.
passages.ot:
Verse 7 quotes God's word to Abraham when Sarah wanted Hagar and Ishmael sent away: “through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (Genesis 21:12). God also promised to care for Ishmael and make him a nation (Genesis 21:13).

Verse 9 joins two promises made to Abraham at his tent: “I will surely return to you at this time next year” (Genesis 18:10) and “At the appointed time I will return to you” (Genesis 18:14).

Verse 12 quotes God's word to Rebecca while the twins struggled in her womb: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated” (Genesis 25:23), and “the older will serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). Notice that God speaks of nations and peoples.

Verse 13 quotes Malachi, written centuries later, near the end of the Old Testament: “Yet Jacob I have loved” (Malachi 1:2) and “but Esau I have hated, and I have made his mountains a wasteland” (Malachi 1:3). Malachi speaks of two nations, Israel and Edom, and of what happened to them in history.
passages.hard:
‘Esau I hated’ needs care. In Hebrew, ‘love’ and ‘hate’ side by side often mean choosing one over the other, not feeling hatred. Jacob ‘loved Rachel more than Leah’, and the next verse calls Leah ‘unloved’ (Genesis 29:30-31). Jesus speaks the same way when he says his followers must ‘hate’ father and mother (Luke 14:26). Malachi's words are covenant language about nations. They are not a word against any person, and nothing here is said against Edomites or anyone else. Israel was told, “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).

Did God choose Jacob over Esau before they were born, and what does Paul mean by it? This is one of the places where faithful Christians disagree. In the Reformed reading, Paul uses Jacob and Esau to show that God's choice of people for salvation rests wholly on his free mercy, not on anything they would do. In the Arminian and Wesleyan reading, and many others, the word to Rebecca is about two nations and their place in history, and Paul's point is that God is free to choose the line through which he works, Gentiles included, not that each person's eternal end is fixed. Some readers on both sides see Paul speaking of peoples as groups; others see him speaking of individuals. The note on verses 19 to 29 says more, and the site's Honest Answer, ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose him?’, lays out both cases. These notes do not settle it.
passages.asks: Paul says the promise came to Jacob ‘not by works but by Him who calls’. Ask what you rely on to feel that you belong to God: your family, your church, your good record. Then ask what it would mean to rest instead on the one who calls.

passages.happening:
Paul hears the objection coming. “What then shall we say? Is God unjust? Certainly not!” (verse 14).

He answers from Scripture. God said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (verse 15). “So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy” (verse 16).

Then the other side. Scripture says to Pharaoh, “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (verse 17).

Paul draws his conclusion: “Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Paul often writes as if he were in a debate. He imagines someone objecting, puts the question in that person's mouth, and answers it. Teachers in the Greek world used this style. ‘Is God unjust?’ is the question any careful hearer would ask after verse 13.

Paul's first answer is about mercy. Mercy, by its nature, is not owed. If it were owed, it would be wages, not mercy. So no one can accuse God of injustice for being merciful. That is the point of verse 16. Mercy does not depend on how much a person wants it or how hard he tries. It depends on the giver.

Then Pharaoh. Every Jewish hearer knew him as the king of Egypt who enslaved Israel and refused to let them go. ‘Hardens’ means making someone stubborn, set against God. Paul says God's dealings with Pharaoh, even his stubbornness, served a purpose: that God's name would be known in all the earth. And it was. Israel sang of it, and the nations heard.

The question these verses raise has never gone away. Paul does not soften it. He goes on to answer a second objection in verse 19.
passages.ot:
Verse 15 quotes Exodus 33. Israel had just worshipped the golden calf. Moses asked, “Please show me Your glory” (Exodus 33:18). God answered by promising to pass by and proclaim his name, and he said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (Exodus 33:19). In its setting this is not a word about turning people away. It is God's answer to a people who deserved nothing, telling them that his mercy is his own free gift. He went on with them.

Verse 17 quotes God's word to Pharaoh before the plague of hail: “But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you” (Exodus 9:16). Paul's wording differs a little from this English, because he follows the Greek translation of the Old Testament with changes of his own. In its setting, God had spared Pharaoh when he could have destroyed him (Exodus 9:15).

Exodus tells the hardening in two ways. Pharaoh hardens his own heart: “he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron” (Exodus 8:15), and again, “But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well” (Exodus 8:32). And God hardens it: “But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exodus 9:12). God had said beforehand, “I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go” (Exodus 4:21). Both are said in Exodus.
passages.hard:
Does God make people stubborn and then blame them? Readers have wrestled with verse 18 for centuries.

Readers in the Reformed tradition hold that God's hardening is his free and just decision. They note that verse 18 puts it as plainly as possible, and that God told Moses he would harden Pharaoh before the plagues began (Exodus 4:21). They also hold that Pharaoh was fully responsible for what he did.

Readers in the Arminian and Wesleyan tradition note the order in the story itself. The first several times, Exodus says Pharaoh's heart was hard or that he hardened it. Only after the sixth plague does the narrator first say that God hardened it (Exodus 9:12). They read God's hardening as his judgment on a man who had already set himself against God: God gave Pharaoh over to what he had chosen, as Romans 1 says God ‘gave them over’.

Both readings keep Pharaoh responsible, and both say God is just. These notes do not choose between them. The book page's hard passage on 9:18 points to both.
passages.asks: Mercy is not owed. That is what makes it mercy. Ask whether you ever speak to God as if he owed you something. Then read verse 16 and thank him for one mercy you did not earn.

passages.t: The potter and the clay, and a people from Jews and Gentiles
passages.happening:
A second objection. “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?” (verse 19).

Paul answers sharply. “But who are you, O man, to talk back to God?” (verse 20). Shall the pot ask the potter, “Why did You make me like this?” (verse 20). The potter has the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use (verse 21).

Then Paul asks a long question he never finishes. “What if God, intending to show His wrath and make His power known, bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction?” (verse 22). What if he did this to make his glory known to the vessels of his mercy, whom he prepared in advance for glory (verse 23), “including us, whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?” (verse 24).

He ends with the prophets. Hosea speaks of God calling ‘My People’ those who were not his people (verses 25-26). Isaiah says “only the remnant will be saved” (verse 27), and that unless the Lord had left them descendants, they would have become like Sodom (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Every house in Rome was full of pottery: jars for oil and grain, lamps, cooking pots, fine dishes for guests. A potter could make a dish for a feast and a pot for kitchen scraps from the same lump of clay. Everyone knew the picture.

Paul's sharp reply in verse 20 is not a refusal to think. It puts the speaker in his place. A creature does not stand over God as his judge. Israel's prophets said the same.

‘Vessels’ means containers, jars or pots. ‘Vessels of His wrath’ may mean those on whom his wrath falls. ‘Prepared for destruction’ does not say who prepared them, and readers differ on that. The ‘vessels of His mercy’ are those God shows mercy to. Notice who they are in verse 24: people called from the Jews and from the Gentiles. Paul's eyes are on the mixed church in Rome. God is making one people from both.

The prophets' words in verses 25 to 29 do two things. Hosea shows God calling people who were not his people. Isaiah shows that, even when most of Israel turned away, God kept a remnant, a faithful few. In both, God's mercy keeps his promise alive.
passages.ot:
The potter and the clay is a picture from the prophets. Isaiah writes, “Shall what is formed say to him who formed it, ‘He did not make me’?” (Isaiah 29:16), and, “Does the clay ask the potter, ‘What are you making?’” (Isaiah 45:9). In Jeremiah 18 the prophet watches a potter whose pot is spoiled, “so he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do” (Jeremiah 18:4). God asks Israel, “can I not treat you as this potter treats his clay?” (Jeremiah 18:6). There the picture is a warning that can change: if the nation turns from evil, God will relent (Jeremiah 18:8).

Verses 25 and 26 quote Hosea. God had named Hosea's children ‘Not My People’ as a sign of judgment on Israel. Then came the promise: “I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people’” (Hosea 2:23), and “in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God’” (Hosea 1:10). Hosea spoke of Israel restored. Paul hears in it also the calling of Gentiles.

Verses 27 to 29 quote Isaiah: “only a remnant will return” (Isaiah 10:22), and “Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, we would have become like Sodom” (Isaiah 1:9).
passages.hard:
Are the ‘vessels of wrath’ people God made for destruction? This is one of the most debated sentences in the Bible. These notes set out three readings and do not choose.

The Reformed reading holds that God chooses, before anyone is born, those he will save, out of his free mercy and not because of anything in them. This is called unconditional election. Those not chosen are left in the sin they freely commit and are justly judged for it. Many in this tradition, using the words of the Westminster Confession of the 1640s, say God was pleased to ‘pass by’ the rest and ‘to ordain them to dishonour and wrath for their sin’. Some call this ‘double predestination’; most of its holders deny that God is the author of anyone's sin.

The Arminian and Wesleyan reading stresses that God ‘bore with great patience’ the vessels of wrath (verse 22). God's patience is meant to lead people to repentance (2:4). These readers hold that people make themselves ready for destruction by persistent refusal, and that God's choosing rests on his knowing who will believe, or on his choice of all who are in Christ by faith.

The corporate reading, held by readers in both traditions, says Paul is speaking of peoples and their roles in God's plan, not of each person's final destiny. His subject is how God has formed one people from Jews and Gentiles (verse 24).

The Honest Answer, ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose him?’, sets out each case.

If you are afraid that you are not chosen, read 8:38-39 slowly. That fear is not usually the mark of someone God has turned away. Paul's own invitation stands open: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul does not answer every question here. He tells a creature to remember that it is a creature. Ask what question you hold against God. Then ask whether you can bring it to him as a child, not as a judge.

passages.happening:
“What then will we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith” (verse 30), “but Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, has not attained it” (verse 31).

Why not? “Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone” (verse 32).

Paul quotes Isaiah: “See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
This is a surprising picture. The Gentiles were not looking for a right standing with God, and they found it. Israel was seeking it with great zeal, and missed it. ‘Righteousness’ here means being in the right with God.

Gentile believers in Rome might hear this and feel proud. Paul will not let them. In chapter 11 he warns them sharply against boasting. And notice what he praises in Israel: they ‘pursued’ righteousness. Paul knew that zeal from the inside. He had been a Pharisee, more zealous than most.

Where did they go wrong? Paul says their pursuit was ‘as if it were by works’, not by faith. The stone they tripped over is Christ. A crucified Messiah was the last thing anyone expected. For many it was a stone to stumble on. For those who trust him, it is a foundation that will not fail.

This stumbling, as Paul will say in 11:11, is not a fall beyond recovery.
passages.ot:
Paul joins two sayings of Isaiah into one. Isaiah 28 says, “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16). There God speaks to Jerusalem's leaders, who trusted in deals with foreign powers instead of in God. The stone is God's sure foundation for those who trust him.

Isaiah 8 says that the LORD himself will be “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isaiah 8:14) to both houses of Israel. There, too, the point is trust: those who fear God will find him a refuge; those who do not will trip over him.

Peter uses the same two verses of Christ (1 Peter 2:6-8). The early church read the stone as the Messiah.
passages.hard:
What does Paul mean by pursuing righteousness ‘as if it were by works’? Readers differ.

Many readers, especially in the Lutheran and Reformed traditions, take it to mean trying to earn a right standing with God by doing what the law commands. Others, often linked with what is called the ‘new perspective on Paul’, take it to mean holding on to the marks of being Jewish, such as circumcision and the food laws, as the boundary of God's people, so that Gentiles could not come in as Gentiles. The book page sets out both readings and does not choose; neither do these notes.

On any reading, this passage gives no one a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people. For centuries some Christians used words like these to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. Paul is a Jew grieving for his people (9:2), and he praises their zeal for God (10:2). The first believers, the apostles, and Jesus himself were Jews. And Paul goes on to say that God has not rejected his people (11:1).
passages.asks: The Gentiles found what they were not looking for. Israel missed what it sought hard. Ask where your own religious effort could become a stone to trip over: where trying hard to be good keeps you from simply trusting Christ.
